articles.text: Last zoo in state to reopen welcomes visitors starting July 29 Oakland Zoo, the last zoo in California to be given authorization to reopen during the coronavirus pandemic, will be opening to the public starting next Wednesday, July 29. The news came on Wednesday, July 15, after a push for it to be reclassified as an outdoor museum. articles.text: A proposed distance-learning model for the coming school year was discussed at length at a special Piedmont School Board meeting on Thursday July 16. In an e-mail message sent on July 14 to parents of Piedmont students, Superintendent Randy Booker announced that the academic year will begin with no in-class instruction, and 100 percent remote learning. With five weeks left before the first day of school, Booker acknowledged that families and faculty need time to prepare for the proposed distance-learning model. This factored into the decision to begin with 100 percent remote learning, he said. “We’re starting with a distance-learning environment, because that is what the conditions are indicating at this point. I would rather start this way, than start in-person and face such a dramatic shift to distance learning,” Booker said. In-person classes would have to be shifted in the event that a student or faculty member were to test positive for COVID-19. Booker acknowledged that the upcoming school year will be “very tumultuous” but held firm that the uptick in coronavirus cases across the state prompted the decision. He also addressed the model that was conducted in the spring and called it “crisis learning” rather than distance-learning. “At first we thought it would be for two weeks, so teachers were organizing lessons, thinking it would be a short period of time. Then [health officers] extended it another month,” Booker said. “That was a lot of crisis planning, learning, training and testing.” A set, consistent bell schedule, where students will have to report to teachers in real-time before class begins, is likely. articles.text: California Interscholastic Federation, the governing body for high school sports in the state, announced on Monday, July 20 an historic change to schedules for all high school sports. There will be no fall sports throughout California, and both fall and winter sports will begin their schedules in January 2021 in response to the global COVID-19 pandemic. Instead of its usual three sports seasons – Fall, Winter and Spring – the CIF has compressed schedules into just two seasons, Winter and Spring. Football, water polo, cross country, and volleyball will have their first day of practice on December 14, with their seasons ending by mid-March. In the spring, Piedmont High will have 10 sports with a total of 17 teams. Girls and boys soccer teams will begin on February 22 – historically the week of the NCS championships, and girls and boys basketball won’t begin until March 15. Girls’ tennis, a fall sport, will be played concurrently with boys’ tennis as a spring sport alongside the boys’ program. This means coaches like Jim Landes and assistant Corey Reich will be pulling double duty. The question of finding extra court and field space remains unanswered, as does the logistical question of providing officials for all sports in the compressed time period. The availability of Witter Field becomes an intriguing question with prospective varsity and JV teams requiring field space. In spring, teams vying for space at Witter will include football, boys’ and girls’ soccer, boys’ and girls’ lacrosse, and track and field.

articles.text: The League of Women Voters of Piedmont will host a discussion on food insecurity in the East Bay, led by Suzan Bateson, Executive Director of the Alameda County Community Food Bank. The event will be livestreamed on the League’s YouTube channel (https://www. youtube.com/channel/UC3v60XGmr13V_9WaYj6qUJg) from 4:00-5:00 p.m. on Tuesday, August 4, 2020. Viewers will learn about Alameda County’s significant food problems which have been exacerbated by COVID-19. Bateson will describe how every citizen can help create a hunger-free community. Bateson, the Food Bank’s Executive Director since 2001, will describe their programs, including fresh food distribution to the community and efforts to eliminate the causes of hunger in the East Bay. During her tenure, the Food Bank has tripled its annual food distribution. In 2016 it won Feeding America’s National Food Bank of the Year Award. The Food Bank has also ended the distribution of carbonated beverages and increased its farm-fresh produce from 1 million to 20 million pounds annually. Bateson was inducted into the Alameda County Women’s Hall of Fame in 2017 and currently is Chair of Feeding America’s Western Region. Viewers may participate on August 4 by submitting questions to the YouTube livestream comment section, or by e-mail to LWVpiedmont@gmail.org. For more information, visit www. lwvpiedmont.org. Find the live stream by searching “League of Women Voters Piedmont” on Youtube.

articles.text: Piedmont City Council approved the first reading of a proposal to implement Reach Codes at a July 20 virtual meeting, with direction for amendments to be explored by staff before a second reading. A package of proposed local amendments to the California Electrical Code, Residential Code, and Building Energy Efficiency Code were considered. The amendments, referred to as “reach codes,” would alter the requirements for home construction and renovation in Piedmont to facilitate building insulation, electrification, and solar panel installation. Staff proposals would set new standards in both new and already existing buildings to reduce gas use and help meet Piedmont’s Climate Action Plan’s goals. “Piedmont adopted a Climate Action Plan first in 2010, and again in 2018 to address this crisis. Actions in the plan include measures to reduce natural gas use, and to increase the use of solar energy systems. The proposed amendments do just that,” said City Planning Director Kevin Jackson. Reach codes, he added, would improve air quality and be cost-effective. Survey results brought to council on July 6 showed that 66 percent of surveyed Piedmonters supported the proposed codes. City staff also held five outreach events in January and February, where amendment ideas were first introduced to residents and contractors for feedback. CivicSpark Fellow Justin Szasz, who will be completing his 11-month fellowship with the city of Piedmont this month, provided detailed information in a presentation to city council members. The proposal, as presented, would require that newly constructed low-rise residential building must use all electric building appliances, and would be prohibited from being connected to natural gas service. This would also apply to new, detached accessory dwelling units. When an existing, low-rise residential building gets a new upper level, or increases its roof area by 30 percent or more, the installation of solar panels is required. Renovations of lowrise residential buildings with a construction value of $25,000 or more must include at least one item from a list of energy efficient insulation or electrification measures. Renovations of $100,000 or more in value must include two of the items. While other jurisdictions have been vocal about wanting to address natural gas use in existing buildings, few have done so. “Piedmont’s proposed amendments will provide leadership to other jurisdictions on this crucial issue,” Szasz said. Results from previous surveys, and information provided by a public engagement program, offered revisions to the proposed amendments that were discussed on July 20. City councilmembers dissected some of the costs associated with the proposal that residents may encounter when renovating. Councilmember Betsy Andersen pointed out that solar panel installation is still a large up-front cost, despite the return in investment after approximately 30 years. She also asked if there would be temporary exemptions for residents who have already been proactive in their sustainable efforts in home improvement. “There are so many folks who keep adopting the incremental changes that they can afford. There are tipping points here where some stuff may become unaffordable with a lot of Piedmonters,” said Vice Mayor Teddy Gray King. Szasz responded by stating that staff believes the proposal to be beneficial to residents, because it meets the climate action plan demands with consideration of upfront costs. “We tried to always make the additional upfront costs proportional to the triggers for the requirements. Because [staff] understands that there is a significant upfront cost for solar panel installation, we weren’t looking at requiring it on every single new roof. We really wanted to hone in on projects that are significantly costly, so it would only be a small increase in the upfront cost,” said Szasz. The goal, he added, is to help residents make these changes without putting any undue cost burden on them. On a 3-2 vote, the council approved a first reading of the proposal, with modifications. Councilmember Anderson and Mayor Bob McBain dissented. The council may hold a second reading on the subject as early as soon as August 3. City staff would then file all amendments to the California Electrical Code and California Energy Code.
articles.title: Council approves first reading of proposed “Reach Codes”

articles.text: FCC further reduces decision-making power of local governments At its meeting on July 20, 2020, the Piedmont City Council joined a coalition to oppose new Federal Communications Commission rules regarding wireless communications facilities. The new rule, approved by the FCC on June 9, 2020, significantly reduces the already limited decision-making power held by local governments to minimize the impact of wireless communication facilities on their community. “We believe there are ways for wireless communication devices to be deployed in an aesthetically appropriate manner. Unfortunately, the FCC seems intent on making that much more difficult, if not impossible,” said Kevin Jackson, Piedmont Planning Director “Unless there is a court-ordered injunction, the new FCC rules will further reduce Piedmont’s ability to control the installation of wireless communication facilities.” Section 6409 of the Spectrum Act requires a city like Piedmont to approve an “eligible facilities request” for a modification of an existing wireless tower or base station that does not “substantially change” the physical dimensions of such tower or base station. The FCC has changed the definition of “substantial change,” as well as other important changes. Changes in the new Eligible Facilities order include, but are not limited to: • The 60-day “shot clock” is now triggered when the applicant takes the first procedural steps, giving the city less time to review for the compliance with the City’s codes. • The definition of concealment has been narrowed so that concealment is only “stealth” design, e.g. look like something other than a wireless tower or base station. Now under the new FCC order, concealment of a facility at a specific location would not include screening by a rooftop or placement behind a tree line or fence. • In addition, the FCC order specif ies that aesthetic requirements or iginally imposed as conditions of approval, such as vegetation cover, fencing, screening, and similar requirements will not be grounds to deny an expressly allowed height or size increase. The order allows the installation of additional antenna up to 20 feet, plus there is no cap to the height of new antenna, for towers outside the public right-of-way. On an existing structure such as a utility pole, the FCC made modifications to the number of equipment cabinets that can be installed per an eligible facilities request. For more information, contact Piedmont Director of Planning and Building Kevin Jackson at kjackson@piedmont.ca.gov. “Someday, son, this vast chain will all belong to you, your mother, your sisters, Uncle Harry or Aunt Lilly Belle.”

pages.text: Wednesday, July 22, 2020 3 News Council approves first reading of proposed “Reach Codes” By Allyson Aleksey Piedmont City Council approved the first reading of a proposal to implement Reach Codes at a July 20 virtual meeting, with direction for amendments to be explored by staff before a second reading. A package of proposed local amendments to the California Electrical Code, Residential Code, and Building Energy Efficiency Code were considered. The amendments, referred to as “reach codes,” would alter the requirements for home construction and renovation in Piedmont to facilitate building insulation, electrification, and solar panel installation. Staff proposals would set new standards in both new and already existing buildings to reduce gas use and help meet Piedmont’s Climate Action Plan’s goals. “Piedmont adopted a Climate Action Plan first in 2010, and again in 2018 to address this crisis. Actions in the plan include measures to reduce natural gas use, and to increase the use of solar energy systems. The proposed amendments do just that,” said City Planning Director Kevin Jackson. Reach codes, he added, would improve air quality and be cost-effective. Survey results brought to council on July 6 showed that 66 percent of surveyed Piedmonters supported the proposed codes. City staff also held five outreach events in January and February, where amendment ideas were first introduced to residents and contractors for feedback. CivicSpark Fellow Justin Szasz, who will be completing his 11-month fellowship with the city of Piedmont this month, provided detailed information in a presentation to city council members. The proposal, as presented, would require that newly constructed low-rise residential building must use all electric building appliances, and would be prohibited from being connected to natural gas service. This would also apply to new, detached accessory dwelling units. When an existing, low-rise residential building gets a new upper level, or increases its roof area by 30 percent or more, the installation of solar panels is required. Renovations of lowrise residential buildings with a construction value of $25,000 or more must include at least one item from a list of energy efficient insulation or electrification measures. Renovations of $100,000 or more in value must include two of the items. While other jurisdictions have been vocal about wanting to address natural gas use in existing buildings, few have done so. “Piedmont’s proposed amendments will provide leadership to other jurisdictions on this crucial issue,” Szasz said. Results from previous surveys, and information provided by a public engagement program, offered revisions to the proposed amendments that were discussed on July 20. City councilmembers dissected some of the costs associated with the proposal that residents may encounter when renovating. Councilmember Betsy Andersen pointed out that solar panel installation is still a large up-front cost, despite the return in investment after approximately 30 years. She also asked if there would be temporary exemptions for residents who have already been proactive in their sustainable efforts in home improvement. “There are so many folks who keep adopting the incremental changes that they can afford. There are tipping points here where some stuff may become unaffordable with a lot of Piedmonters,” said Vice Mayor Teddy Gray King. Szasz responded by stating that staff believes the proposal to be beneficial to residents, because it meets the climate action plan demands with consideration of upfront costs. “We tried to always make the additional upfront costs proportional to the triggers for the requirements. Because [staff] understands that there is a significant upfront cost for solar panel installation, we weren’t looking at requiring it on every single new roof. We really wanted to hone in on projects that are significantly costly, so it would only be a small increase in the upfront cost,” said Szasz. The goal, he added, is to help residents make these changes without putting any undue cost burden on them. On a 3-2 vote, the council approved a first reading of the proposal, with modifications. Councilmember Anderson and Mayor Bob McBain dissented. The council may hold a second reading on the subject as early as soon as August 3. City staff would then file all amendments to the California Electrical Code and California Energy Code. Piedmont joins coalition of cities opposing FCC rules on wireless communications FCC further reduces decision-making power of local governments At its meeting on July 20, 2020, the Piedmont City Council joined a coalition to oppose new Federal Communications Commission rules regarding wireless communications facilities. The new rule, approved by the FCC on June 9, 2020, significantly reduces the already limited decision-making power held by local governments to minimize the impact of wireless communication facilities on their community. “We believe there are ways for wireless communication devices to be deployed in an aesthetically appropriate manner. Unfortunately, the FCC seems intent on making that much more difficult, if not impossible,” said Kevin Jackson, Piedmont Planning Director “Unless there is a court-ordered injunction, the new FCC rules will further reduce Piedmont’s ability to control the installation of wireless communication facilities.” Section 6409 of the Spectrum Act requires a city like Piedmont to approve an “eligible facilities request” for a modification of an existing wireless tower or base station that does not “substantially change” the physical dimensions of such tower or base station. The FCC has changed the definition of “substantial change,” as well as other important changes. Changes in the new Eligible Facilities order include, but are not limited to: • The 60-day “shot clock” is now triggered when the applicant takes the first procedural steps, giving the city less time to review for the compliance with the City’s codes. • The definition of concealment has been narrowed so that concealment is only “stealth” design, e.g. look like something other than a wireless tower or base station. Now under the new FCC order, concealment of a facility at a specific location would not include screening by a rooftop or placement behind a tree line or fence. • In addition, the FCC order specif ies that aesthetic requirements or iginally imposed as conditions of approval, such as vegetation cover, fencing, screening, and similar requirements will not be grounds to deny an expressly allowed height or size increase. The order allows the installation of additional antenna up to 20 feet, plus there is no cap to the height of new antenna, for towers outside the public right-of-way. On an existing structure such as a utility pole, the FCC made modifications to the number of equipment cabinets that can be installed per an eligible facilities request. For more information, contact Piedmont Director of Planning and Building Kevin Jackson at kjackson@piedmont.ca.gov. articles.text: An issue with paperwork and variance approvals caused Alameda County to shut down outdoor dining for the second time, only to allow restaurants to reopen again last weekend. After months of being limited to providing takeout and delivery only, the county re-opened for sitdown dining on June 19. But on Friday, July 13, new guidance from the state made clear that the county did not file all necessary paperwork required to reopen. On Saturday in the middle of the day, restaurant owners were blindsided by an abrupt order to close. “I saw it on the 11 o’clock news [on Friday],” said Alan Carlson, owner of Italian Colors, a popular restaurant in Montclair Village. “We didn’t get a robocall [from the county], no email, nothing,” he said. Like other restaurant owners, Carlson brought employees out of furlough to work, adding to the confusion. With outdoor dining eliminated, he was worried he would have to furlough those same employees again. “It breaks your heart to have to do that. They’ve been off for three, almost four months,” Carlson said. Luckily, the county rushed Alan Carlson, owner of Italian Colors, prepares dinners for guests pre-COVID-19. to complete paperwork that would allow for outdoor dining. Restaurant owners in Alameda County were in limbo for about five days. On Wednesday afternoon, July 15, public health officials announced that outdoor dining once again could resume in the county after the state approved a variance to proceed. All restaurants in the county that can adequately provide socially-distant outdoor dining areas now may do so. Restaurants are still allowed to conduct takeout and delivery operations.

articles.text: Fenton’s Creamery on Piedmont Avenue, Piedmont’s s iconic ice cream parlor since 1894, has endured wars, depressions, and earthquakes without once having to shut down their ice cream plant. Only a fire closed them temporarily for rebuilding. And then came COVID-19. Scott Whidden and his family have owned Fenton’s since 1987, when they bought the business from a national dairy corporation to bring it back to local ownership. Fenton’s has a large following and is beloved by many for providing a perfect atmosphere for celebrations, nostalgia and indulgence. When COVID-19’s shelter-inplace went into effect and Fenton’s was given permission to serve only takeout, they were in a spot of trouble. Takeout normally accounts for 20 percent of their business, and parties bring in half of the total revenue. They had to furlough 40 of their 65 workers and encouraged them to file for unemployment. In April when it became clear the pandemic was not going away, the furloughs turned into layoffs. Whidden said, “It is ghastly. These are people that have worked at Fenton’s for 10-15 years. We don’t want to fire anyone. They are a part of the Fenton’s family.” Fenton’s does have some advantages, however. It has two sets of double doors at the entry, making for an easy flow in and out now. And they have 24 seats outdoors with benches and tables in the parking lot. They can accommodate a lot After shutting down ice cream production for the first time since a fire many years ago, Fenton’s Creamery is back serving ice cream and food for takeout. It is offering delivery and outdoor dining on an expanded patio on the parking lot. of people and maintain the county’s required six-foot distancing. They have expanded their delivery service, mostly through Doordash, and their website allows for easy ordering and payment for pickup. With these revenues they have been able to return to roughly half of their normal production. “At 50 percent, we are at a self-sustaining level,” said Whidden. “But in terms of economics, we are losing week over week, just because of the size of the building and its overhead. We will have to tread water probably until Spring Break 2021, hopefully not beyond that.” “If this is a ‘new normal’, we have to ask the question, ‘Does Fenton’s even need a party room or dining room?’ To cue up just for takeout, that would be tragic,” he said. “Our essential workers are basically putting their lives at risk to serve a scoop of ice cream. It’s mind-boggling to get your arms around that. But that is the reality of it.” Fenton’s may be in the food industry, but they are also in the entertainment business. Going to Fenton’s has always been an event – a celebration. “Ice cream is like a sweet, reminisce treat for people. Sitting there and being a part of that carnival of activities is a big part of it. People come to celebrate what is going on with them or just park themselves to indulge a little bit,” said Whidden.

articles.text: California Governor Gavin Newsom At a press briefing on Friday, July 17, California Gov. Gavin Newsom issued strict guidelines for reopening schools across the state. School can only open for in-person classes if their county has been off the state’s watch list for two weeks. Schools that don’t meet those criteria must begin with classes this fall with distance learning. Alameda County leads the Bay Area in total COVID-19 cases and is on the state’s watch list, delaying some anticipated re-openings. On Friday morning, San Francisco County was also added to the state’s coronavirus watch list. San Francisco, Oakland, and Sacramento school districts all have announced plans to begin school in August with remote learning. If school districts in the state want to reopen, their county health officials must prove two weeks of declining coronavirus cases. Districts that may reopen would require all school staff and students in 3rd grade and above to wear masks and with desks six feet apart. Staff members are also expected to keep a six-foot distance from students. Piedmont School District made the decision to begin the academic year virtually and proposed a distance-learning model at a July 16 school board meeting. “Since we’ve issued our guidance, conditions have changed dramatically,” State Superintendent of Public Instruction Tony Thurmond said during a media briefing last Wednesday, July 15, adding that he expects more districts will decide to begin the term virtually. “In any place where there is uncertainty, we should proceed with caution. In many cases, that’s going to [mean] distance learning.” Thurmond initially left the decision to reopen schools up to individual school districts throughout the state. articles.text: Jenessa Joffe, a 1994 Piedmont High graduate, recently directed and co-produced a second season of the award-winning digital series “Radical Cram School.” The short Youtube videos address social activism with kids by way of host Kristina Wong, a San Francisco comedian and performance artist. Radical Cram School is a kid-centric, entertaining and informative series that empowers Asian girls and kids of all ethnicities color to embrace their identities, fight for social justice, and be the revolution. For Joffe, this project feels just right. “I’m a storyteller and I love comedy. To be able mix those with social activism feels like the truest expression of who I am and who I want to be in the world,” Joffe said. The episodes involve kids enrolled as Young Rebels in “Radical Cram School” which engages in difficult topics like undocumented migration, the Black Lives Matter protest and gender identity. Some of the episodes have a format in which kids provide the dialogue for Wong, who lip-synchs a costumed reenactment on fun sets utilizing puppets. Joffe sees a current demand for comedic activism. “I think there is a call now for content that is giving a way for kids to talk about some of these issues they have been wondering about. Kids are going to protests and they are seeing things on TV and they are wondering, ‘Why are they wearing masks?’” “You can’t hide things from kids,” Joffe added. The show got its start last year with crowdfunding as financial support. It now has a fan club, so it raised even more money for its second season. Joffe is pitching the series as a TV show through “Yes. And Laughter Lab,” which allows the show to be viewed by film and entertainment professionals like Comedy Central as well as social justice organizations. Joffe has seen a shift in the nonprofit entertainment world. “More and more social justice organizations and nonprofits are wanting to hire comedy people to make content because they Director and Producer Jenessa Joffe (right) with Creator and Host Kristina Wong and Producers Anna Michelle Wang and Teddy Chao at the Season 2 premiere party for “Radical Cram School.” realize that people will pay more attention when it is entertainment. Maybe Jon Stewart was the first big one to do it,” Joffe said. “Comedy has the power to open people’s hearts and allow us to make a change internally that is non-violent and uplifting. That’s why I’m attracted to it, it’s pretty powerful actually,” she added. This current project aims to create space for voices often underrepresented in public conversations. The series can be used as a fun resource to spark conversation with kids about identity, civil rights, and progressive values. Radical Cram School zooms in on social changes through the lens of Asian-American identity and female empowerment but explores many hot topics. Joffe admitted that with this project, she feels good about her career as a director and producer. Her advice to young people interested in a career in film? “Start making films and never stop; that’s really all there is,” she stated. “You will find likeminded people by making films with others, and that’s how you build a community.” Joffe’s collection of videos can be viewed at www.jenessajoffe.com and Radical Cram School via Youtube, and on www.jenessajoffe.com/projects/ radical-cram-school.

To be able mix those with social activism feels like the truest expression of who I am and who I want to be in the world,” Joffe said. The episodes involve kids enrolled as Young Rebels in “Radical Cram School” which engages in difficult topics like undocumented migration, the Black Lives Matter protest and gender identity. Some of the episodes have a format in which kids provide the dialogue for Wong, who lip-synchs a costumed reenactment on fun sets utilizing puppets. Joffe sees a current demand for comedic activism. “I think there is a call now for content that is giving a way for kids to talk about some of these issues they have been wondering about. Kids are going to protests and they are seeing things on TV and they are wondering, ‘Why are they wearing masks?’” “You can’t hide things from kids,” Joffe added. The show got its start last year with crowdfunding as financial support. It now has a fan club, so it raised even more money for its second season. Joffe is pitching the series as a TV show through “Yes. And Laughter Lab,” which allows the show to be viewed by film and entertainment professionals like Comedy Central as well as social justice organizations. Joffe has seen a shift in the nonprofit entertainment world. “More and more social justice organizations and nonprofits are wanting to hire comedy people to make content because they Director and Producer Jenessa Joffe (right) with Creator and Host Kristina Wong and Producers Anna Michelle Wang and Teddy Chao at the Season 2 premiere party for “Radical Cram School.” realize that people will pay more attention when it is entertainment. Maybe Jon Stewart was the first big one to do it,” Joffe said. “Comedy has the power to open people’s hearts and allow us to make a change internally that is non-violent and uplifting. That’s why I’m attracted to it, it’s pretty powerful actually,” she added. This current project aims to create space for voices often underrepresented in public conversations. The series can be used as a fun resource to spark conversation with kids about identity, civil rights, and progressive values. Radical Cram School zooms in on social changes through the lens of Asian-American identity and female empowerment but explores many hot topics. Joffe admitted that with this project, she feels good about her career as a director and producer. Her advice to young people interested in a career in film? “Start making films and never stop; that’s really all there is,” she stated. “You will find likeminded people by making films with others, and that’s how you build a community.” Joffe’s collection of videos can be viewed at www.jenessajoffe.com and Radical Cram School via Youtube, and on www.jenessajoffe.com/projects/ radical-cram-school. articles.text: Bruno Banuelos As middle schoolers with a lot of time on our hands, we want to make sure we are spending some of it helping others. We are lucky enough to have a program in our community that gives us the ability to give back to people who are less fortunate. The Piedmont Service Club (PSC), affiliated with Piedmont Community Service Crew (for high schoolers), connects middle schoolers to service opportunities in nearby neighborhoods. Under normal circumstances we participate in events that range from tutoring refugee kids to volunteering at local plant nurseries, among other activities. Since it is not currently safe to meet in person, the club has found new ways to serve the community. We decided to take advantage of an event that took place on June 6 which had crew members collectively cook a meal for 75 needy people, but cook from our own homes. Through a carefully planned sign-up, we chose which meal components we wanted to prepare. Then we packed up our food and drove it to the College Avenue Presbyterian Church in Oakland where it was packaged into individual dinner boxes so the recipients could take it with them. As we carried the food to the serving tables on the side of the church, we saw the homeless people sitting on the steps waiting to be served and felt sympathy for them. We all felt grateful for the opportunity to help them. Despite it being hard work, we felt a sense of reward knowing that we were helping provide meals to people who needed them. COVID-19 makes it difficult to find ways to volunteer right now, but this is one way to make a big impact on many people’s lives. It is more important now than ever that we come together as a community and support each other. If you find you want to use your time to help others, join the Piedmont Service Club, an organization for 6th, 7th and 8th graders, or if you are in high school, join the Piedmont Community Service Crew. You will meet a group of students who are like-minded, motivated, and dedicated to serving their community. For more information, contact Crew Advisor Ken Li at ken.i.li@ sbcglobal.net or visit the website: https://www.pcservicecrew.org/

articles.text: Part 2 in a 3-part series. Previously published in the Post on March 28, 2018 Out of Portugal’s Bairrada region come two local gastronomic points of pride. One is the grape varietal baga, which requires a stubborn devotion on the part of wine producers and something of an open mind from the wine drinker. The other is leitão, an ovenroasted suckling pig. On our first day, a tasting with winemaker Mario Sergio, carrying on the third generation at Quinta das Bágeiras, turned into an invitation for lunch. At Mugasa, the hot spot to eat and pass an afternoon in the one-rotary town of Fogueira, we had the opportunity to sample Bairrada’s delicacies as they were meant to be – enjoyed together. Our caravan to Mugasa included Mario, his assistant Ana and his wife, their five friends visiting from Luxembourg and Basel, and 10 open bottles from that morning’s tasting. Our little international coalition, along with our oversized ice bucket that included a 1991 bottle of espumante (sparkling wine) took over a corner table of the top floor. Espumante finds a nice home in Bairrada, with its cool climate, clay soils and the acidic baga. The dishes came out family style, with the leitão as the centerpiece. It was a type of Thanksgiving, with the leitão taking the place of the turkey. All differences in nationality or language were set aside to come together in the commonality of sharing good food and wine. The next day was spent with Luís Pato, known as Bairrada’s “rebel” and something of a living legend for infusing traditional baga with enough modernity to bring this beloved, if somewhat difficult, grape to the world’s attention. Highly tannic, baga can be harsh when young and traditionally requires many years in the bottle to mellow and reveal its other notes of dark fruits. Most markets do not have such patience to allow baga its proper aging. The trick to softening a grape like baga is to add oak, always a controversial subject as it unleashes a long list of choices on the part of winemakers. appellation. Luís, a chemical engineer by training, took the lead in 1980 and began tinkering with modern techniques and outside methods. Luís managed to find the sweet spot. His father, João, became the first in the region, in 1970, to bottle under his own name after Bairrada was made a distinct everyone could see – and taste – the diamond in the rough. articles.text: No fall sports; Football starts in Jan.; basketball, soccer now spring sports; boys’ & girls’ tennis to resume in spring Staff Photos Sports at Witter Field is officially set to return in January 2021, starting with football. On Monday, July 20, the California Interscholastic Federation (CIF) and North Coast Section (NCS) announced their sports calendar for the 2020-2021 school year. In an historic decision, the CIF ruled there will be no fall high school sports in California. Traditional fall sports, such as football, cross-country, water polo and volleyball, will begin in January 2021 The customary three sport seasons – fall, winter and spring – will be condensed into two seasons, late winter and spring. “In examining the most effective way to deliver Fall, Winter and Spring sports for the 2020- 2021 school year, the decision was made to condense three seasons of sport into two seasons, primarily to help with the spacing between particular sports and the overlap of certain sports between seasons,” wrote NCS commissioner Pat Cruikshank in a July 20 press release. Cruikshank noted that NCS is aiming at completing a full season for each sport, which, given its history of playoff scheduling blunders was refreshing to hear. This means sports like football will have 10 weeks to play 10 games. “It is important to point out that no reduction in the number of contests has taken place, meaning that a sport that generally allows 24 contests and 2 scrimmages during a normal season is still allowed the same number of contests. We hope that this allows all schools the opportunity to attempt to play a full schedule, albeit in some cases during a smaller window,” he continued. Fall sports that would typically begin action next month will have their official first date of practice set for Monday, DecemBaseball at Humphries Diamond will return in April for its start of play. ber 14. Each season is anticipated to stretch until late-March, including football, cross country, volleyball, and water polo. Although this will be the latest North Coast Section football playoffs in history, it is not uncharted waters for the Southern Section, which held its football championship in March 1919 due to the Spanish Flu. Spring sports’ start of practice is scheduled to for the last week of February and early March. Here’s a further look at the effects of the new CIF sports calendar: Get Ready for Spring: 10 sports, 17 varsity teams New spring sports: both soccer teams, girls’ tennis, and both basketball programs have their official start of practice set to February 22, March 8, and March 15 respectively. Other active sports at Piedmont from February 22 to lateJune will include: badminton, both swim teams, boys’ tennis, baseball, both golf teams, both lacrosse, softball, and track and field. Aside from the expected date change, the largest change will be girls’ tennis getting moved from fall to spring and being assigned to play a single season concurrently with boys’ tennis. Many questions arise, starting with the number of courts available, their locations, and how veteran coach Jim Landes and assistant coach Corey Reich will be able to coach two teams concurrently. He’s still waiting for the NCS plans on the variables for schools like Piedmont with limited court space. “They haven’t told me any details as to how the seasons are going to work in February,” said Landes. “It just says boys’ and girls’ seasons start then. They haven’t said whether it will be a co-ed team or somehow run them simultaneously. I don’t know,” said Landes. Should both boys’ and girls’ programs run at the same time in separate seasons, Landes points out an obvious factor that each coach at the school is worried about, field-space. “Running both teams is going to be difficult with only four courts. If we keep teams around the same size, I would need all four courts for each practice. We’d have to do one practice followed by another, and you have to consider time availability of the tennis courts and school hours for kids. I’ll just have to be flexible,” he said. Landes could see this resulting in the JV programs dissolving given the lack of space at the Corey Reich Tennis Center. Landes is expecting 15 incoming freshmen to play when the season starts. “With this many kids, we may not be able to have a JV team. I’m worried about kids who may miss out on playing. articles.text: For many in the football world, these fall months will be the first without the sport for the first time since their childhood. The California Interscholastic Federation announced on Monday that due to COVID-19, Fall sports will not begin until next January. So this week, with football at Witter Field arriving the latest in school history, we’re going back – way back. In 1976, coach Bob Muenter’s Highlanders were a powerhouse in the East Bay and winners of the school’s only football North Coast Section championship. It was Muenter’s final year as coach before becoming the school’s athletic director until 1983. Muenter, the namesake of the PHS Football’s Perpetual Spirit Award, led the football program from 1950-1976, building championship teams in 1959, 1960, 1965, and 1972. The team known as Muenter’s Boys went undefeated in 1976 in winning the Alameda County Athletic League title, then went on to win the North Coast Section 2A championship with a 14-7 win over the Sunset High of Hayward, a school that closed in 1990. Jeff Dreher was a part of the program, the honorary namesake of PHS’ Most Valuable Offensive Lineman award. Another Piedmont Sports Hall of Famer Jeff Haile was a member of the 1976 team. For this week’s look back in Piedmont sports history, we examine the NCS champion 1976 football team and its legendary coach, Bob Muenter member of the Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame, running back and linebacker Jeff Haile, was the league’s Player of the Year in ‘76. Haile was also an All-League track and field athlete in shotput and is the school’s record holder in the event. He went on to play football and rugby for Stanford and was elected to the Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame in 2014. Thanks to footage on YouTube we can witness Haile barreling through the line in games against Encinal, San Leandro, Miramonte, and Albany on the way to the NCS Championship at Pacific Field in San Leandro, now Burrell Field. While Haile made headlines as Piedmont’s premier running back, Muenter’s defense was the hallmark with a rough, efficient style that is reminiscent of Jack Tatum’s and George Atkinson’s Oakland Raiders of the 1970s. Using a 4-3 defense that is still used by pro-teams, the Highlanders were seemingly in the backfield on every play, tackling quarterbacks and running backs with frequent blitzes. The school reached the NCS semifinals in 1981 in a 28-14 loss to San Lorenzo, and 2014 under coach Scott Coats after posting the school’s best record in football, 12-1 and a league championship (WACC Shoreline). Entered as the No. 2 seed, they were upset by No. 3 Justin-Siena 14-3. Two years later, 2016, the team also advanced to the NCS semifinals.

articles.text: It’s been an offseason unlike any other for football teams throughout the country. So far this summer, NFL, college, and prep-teams have all been in the same boat: processing information and learning, but none of it on a football field due to the continuing coronavirus pandemic. “We’re doing as much Zoom as possible given it’s a non-contact situation. We’re doing a lot of teaching online; that’s how we’ve been doing our summer prepping,” explained PHS head coach Jerome Johnson “It’s really educational football; it’s all about teaching, all about the fundamentals and principals of offense and defense,” said Johnson, who is set to embark on his second season at the helm. The name constantly heard with sports’ programs this summer: Zoom, the virtual meeting app designed for camera-based chat rooms. Basically, every football team – big to small, professional to amateur – have been utilizing Zoom for their sessions. “We can really go step-bystep. As weird as it may seem, it’s almost better, because we have a captive audience. Kids are engaged, ask a lot of questions and we can go over so many nuances of teaching the game of football,” described Johnson. While at this time last year, helmets and pads would be cracking at Witter Field with annual scrimmages at Laney College and Miramonte. Now, without Xs and Os being taught on the sidelines or on a chalkboard, student-athletes are putting their brains to work instead of legs. “Now the teachable moments are unique. Usually during the summer, kids have a lot of open space and are more engaged with each other instead of paying attention within a classroom setting,” said Johnson. “The advantage of what we’re doing is putting players in certain situations and have them draw up the offensive or defensive scheme based on what we’re asking them. When you put them in scenarios mentally, we hope it will translate when we hit the field,” he added. articles.text: Photo by Cory Weaver German soprano Nadja Michael sings the lead in Janacek’s The Makropulos Case. Each week, the San Francisco Opera streams an archived opera as part of its “Opera is On” virtual streaming series. This Saturday, July 25, Leos Janacek’s The Makropulos Case will be streaming for 24 hours. More than 300 years ago an alchemist named Makropulos was employed by the Hapsburg Emperor Rudolf II to create an elixir to give the Emperor eternal life. Not trusting Makropulos’s finished potion, the Emperor forced him to administer it to his own daughter, Elina. When she became seriously ill Makropulos was put in prison, but Elina eventually recovered and escaped. What was not apparent at the time was that the elixir actually worked, granting Elina some 300 additional years of life. During the time that she has lived, Elina has had many identities, many names (always with the initials E.M.), and many affairs. One of her more passionate affairs was with Baron Josef Ferdinand Prus, by whom she had a son. While Prus left his estate in writing to this illegitimate son, the will has long gone missing and there has ensued a century-long dispute between two branches of the family, Gregor and Prus, over rights to the estate. The opera, originally premiered during the 2016–17 season, is sung in Czech with English supertitles. To view this weekend’s upcoming opera, visit https://sfopera. com/opera-is-on/?gclid=Cj0KCQjw9b_4BRCMARIsADMUIyrjmT3GiYT7kJ28ktDf5CQl23ZdBV36DGcghIUs_PUUv53FsP- 3m864aAoTTEALw_wcB. Donors and subscribers can still stream past productions of Mephistopheles, The Capulets and the Montagues, Moby-Dick, and Lucrezia Borgia by logging on to their account on SFopera.com.

articles.text: Liam Neeson and Julianne Moore in a scene from Chloe. Movie review by Chris Honoré To suggest that Chloe is simply an erotic thriller is to diminish what is an intriguing film – a character study and examination of a woman’s attempt to bridge what seems an insurmountable distance between herself and her husband. At its center, the story is not about seduction but about abiding loneliness, perhaps best captured by those stark scenes where Catherine (Julianne Moore), a successful gynecologist in Toronto, stands looking out the window at the street below, gazing at her husband as he sits in his den working on his computer, and as she observes her patients in the waiting room. She is suffused with a feeling of disconnection, as if all she has known is now inaccessible, emotionally elusive. She has grown older. She feels less desirable. Her viewpoint has grown clinical. Because she and her husband, David (Liam Neeson), a professor of music, married some 20 years, have lost contact, and she observes him being flirtatious with his students and with other women, she suspects he is having an affair. What she does at this moment, at this intersection in her life, is profoundly human and understandable, but immensely destructive. She hires a young prostitute, Chloe (Amanda Seyfried), to test her husband’s fidelity and sets in motion a series of events filled with unintended consequences. She she insists that Chloe report back to her the details of her time with David. Unexpectedly, Catherine finds herself in the position of a voyeur, more comfortable with hearing about and imagining the intimacy shared by Chloe and David than searching for a path toward intimacy herself. But then isn’t her voyeurism the handmaiden to pornography? Ultimately she finds nothing satisfying about hearing about David and Chole, and yet she cannot stop herself. She might have hired a private detective, of course, but then perhaps she was looking for something else, something she divines from the outset. There are no substitutes, no amount of triangulation will ever point the way back, though Catherine tries – at great risk and potentially great harm, to herself and her family. Chloe has its moments as a studied thriller, and it spirals nicely toward a taught conclusion. Some might find the premise far-fetched, balking at the idea that any professional, highly educated woman would make such an extreme choice. But an aspect of truth is seen in Moore’s portrayal of Catherine that sustains the film, a portrayal supported by the fine performances of Liam Neeson and Amanda Seyfried, who is perfectly cast in the role of the young seductress Chloe. Chloe. Starring Julianne Moore, Amanda Seyfried, Liam Neeson and Max Thierot. Directed by Atom Egoyan. Rated R. Originally published in the Post on March 31, 2010. articles.text: Jennifer Lawrence in a scene from Winter’s Bone. Mobie review by Chris Honoré The first stark images of Winter’s Bone are of two children playing in a yard, surrounded by trees winter bare, the sunlight diffuse, without warmth. The house is more a shack than not, wood frame and hard used. Dead cars and appliances sit deep in weeds. The setting is a hamlet in the southern Missouri Ozarks, a place apart, where people – hard scrabble, insular – live on the frayed edges of society. Many are off the grid, suspicious, even paranoid, their source of income the cooking and sale of methamphetamine. The children in the yard, a brother and sister, are the siblings of Ree Dooly, 17 (played by Jennifer Lawrence), who carries the full weight of her family. Her mother is paralyzed by a deep depression and her father, Jessup, recently arrested for cooking meth, has just made bond and been released from jail. What Ree soon learns from the local sheriff is that in order to post bond, Jessup has put up the house and the surrounding acreage, some of it rich with timber, as collateral. If he fails to make his court date all will be forfeited. She and her family will be homeless. Ree sets out to find her father, a journey that takes her to the center of the Dolly clan where she discovers that family ties will only protect her to a certain point and no further. She’s told to leave it alone by men and women who look at her with cold eyes and grimly set mouths, their secrets impenetrable. For Ree, the stakes are high, finding her father crucial, and she’s prepared to risk all. Winter’s Bone is a remarkable film, one of the best thus far in a paper thin, spring-summer season. The performance by Lawrence is astonishing as she captures with a steely grittiness the intractable place in which Ree finds herself. As a character, Ree is the anchor of her family, a person who faces a reality she barely understands. Lawrence demonstrates an uncanny subtlety and power in her portrayal, considering that the dialogue is laconic, stripped of all excess language. So authentic is this film that it borders on cinema-verite’. As the story unfolds, it’s easy to forget the actors are not locals but are delivering exceptional performances. At its core, Winter’s Bone is a woman’s film. For all of their truculence and need to control, leavened with a subtext of violence, the men are almost peripheral. It’s the women, and, of course, Ree, who are central to the events as they slowly, ominously develop. It’s the women who place Ree in harm’s way. This fact gives the story an interesting and compelling dimension. If you love movies that illuminate, films that are an unsettling and penetrating window into the human condition, Winter’s Bone is not to be missed. Winter’s Bone. Starring Jennifer Lawrence, John Hawkes, Dale Dickey and Garret Dillahunt. Directed by Debra Granik. Rated R. Originally published in the Post on July 28, 2010. articles.title: Winter’s Bone a stunning, realistic film

articles.text: An image from the film How to Train Your Dagon: The Hidden World. How to Train Your Dragon: The Hidden World is the last installment of what has been a very successful franchise, first released in 2010. This final wrap may lack the punchy and fresh stories of the first two, but it is beautifully animated with glorious scenes of dragons in flight, all circling the island refuge of Berk. This medieval village is home to a cohort of Vikings, now led by the aspirational chief, Hiccup (Jay Baruchel), and supported by his girlfriend, Astrid (America Ferrera). It is filled with characters both young and old and is wonderful. Hiccup’s best friend, Toothless, who is a special breed of alpha dragon, is alive and well and the two still ride the skies as one. The computer graphics are breathtaking. This is distinctly not your grandfather’s painstaking, Disneyesque animation. Naturally there is a villain, a malevolent dragon hunter called Grimmel (F. Murray Abraham) who speaks with a strange accent. His mission is to kill Toothless and take control of the dragons living peacefully in Berk. Luckily, he’s a bit of a klutz – good at planning, not so much at execution. Unexpectedly, two budding love stories surface. One is telegraphed in the previous films, a romance between Hiccup and Astrid (they’re now talking marriage). The other is between Toothless and a kindred young female dragon, who, unlike the obsidian Toothless, is white as the driven snow. I wondered how these two story lines would work since the audience is decidedly young, not even teenagers. I did find the dialogue charming, nicely contemporized, though I don’t think Hiccup ever says or even whispers the word “Dude!” The final act, which takes Hiccup and Astrid to the Hidden World, is remarkable – a veritable feast of color. Having found this place at the edge of the world, Hiccup realizes that there is a safe place for Toothless and his love interest. Separation is now inevitable – or maybe not. There’s enough in this film for the youngsters to have the chance to fully say goodbye to a nifty crew of dragon riders and their dragons. How to Train Your Dragon: The Hidden World. Animated with the voices of Jay Baruchel, America Ferrera, and F. Murray Abraham. Directed by Dean DuBlois. 1 hr., 50 min. Rated PG. Originally published in the Post on March 6, 2019.

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré The template for Brave is decidedly familiar, which is surprising for Pixar, a studio that has pioneered computer-generated animation with original and compelling stories (Wall-E, Ratatouille, The Incredibles). Brave is, nevertheless, a beautifully rendered work, an example of detailed and sumptuous animation that creates breathtaking scenes as its heroine, Princess Merida (Kelly Macdonald), rides her Clydesdale Angus through the emerald green countryside of 10th century Scotland. What makes Brave familiar is the tension between the headstrong teenager, Merida – wildly spirited, with tangled persimmon-colored hair, a deadeye archer, possessing an unyielding wish to fashion her own destiny – and her mother, Queen Elinor (Emma Thompson), who wishes only that her rebellious daughter behave as a demure, corseted, wimple-covered princess should. By Chris Honore’ How to Train Your Dragon: The Hidden World is the last installment of what has been a very successful franchise, first released in 2010. This final wrap may lack the punchy and fresh stories of the first two, but it is beautifully animated with glorious scenes of dragons in flight, all circling the island refuge of Berk. This medieval village is home to a cohort of Vikings, now led by the aspirational chief, Hiccup (Jay Baruchel), and supported by his girlfriend, Astrid (America Ferrera). It is filled with characters both young and old and is wonderful. Hiccup’s best friend, Toothless, who is a special breed of alpha dragon, is alive and well and the two still ride the skies as one. The computer graphics are breathtaking. This is distinctly not your grandfather’s painstaking, Disneyesque animation. Naturally there is a villain, a malevolent dragon hunter called Grimmel (F. Murray Abraham) who speaks with a strange accent. His mission is to kill Toothless and take control of the dragons living peacefully in Berk. Luckily, he’s a bit of a klutz – good at planning, not so much at execution. Unexpectedly, two budding love stories surface. One is telegraphed in the previous films, a romance between Hiccup and Astrid (they’re now talking marriage). The other is between Toothless and a kindred young female dragon, who, unlike the obsidian Toothless, is white as the driven snow. I wondered how these two story lines would work since the audience is decidedly young, not even teenagers. I did find the dialogue charming, nicely contemporized, though I don’t think Hiccup ever says or even whispers the word “Dude!” The final act, which takes Hiccup and Astrid to the Hidden World, is remarkable – a veritable feast of color. Having found this place at the edge of the world, Hiccup realizes that there is a safe place for Toothless and his love interest. Separation is now inevitable – or maybe not. There’s enough in this film for the youngsters to have the chance to fully say goodbye to a nifty crew of dragon riders and their dragons. How to Train Your Dragon: The Hidden World. articles.text: Let me pose a question to you. Is classical music relevant in today’s world? The devotees are diminishing and with it, the market. Those are the facts. So, what is so popular in pop music? Thump, Thump, Thump, Thump etc, ad infinitum. And don’t forget one TWO, one TWO, one TWO etc. ad infinitum. And, as for lyrics, a steady stream of profanity - all spoken in monotone. Not sung. Monotone speech. Wow! The knock against classical music is that it is boring. Thump, Thump, Thump, Thump etc. ad infinitum one TWO, one TWO, one TWO etc. ad infinitum. I ask you, which is boring? A friend observed that pop music always accents the second beat. How boring is that? one TWO, one TWO, one TWO etc. ad infinitum. Compare the utter predictability (i.e. boring) rhythm of pop music with multi- hued classical music. Take, for example, a 3-beat rhythm. The nobility of the Polonaise, the whirling lightness of the quick Viennese waltz, the elegant regularity of the Minuet, the second beat emphasis of the slow Sarabande, or the third-beat emphasis of the Mazurka… and that’s just the tip of the iceberg. Versus... Thump, Thump, Thump, Thump etc. ad infinitum one TWO, one TWO, one TWO etc. ad infinitum. Psychiatrists and psychologists have studied the effects of classical music on the general public. The “Mozart effect” is not a psychological fantasy. Listening to classical music actually makes us smarter. It does. Playing it is even better. While pop music (whether rock, heavymetal, hip-hop, or rap) beats us into intellectual Dementia Pugilistica, classical music, by its very nature, encourages thought and imagination. For those of you who think classical music is boring, I will leave you to your Thump, Thump, Thump, Thump etc. ad infinitum one TWO, one TWO, one TWO etc ad infinitum. As for me, give me Bach and Mozart and Beethoven. NEXT WEEK: Where do we go from here? The nuances of nature. Are they needed in music? Just listen to Beethoven’s Symphony No. 6, the “Pastorale.”
articles.title: An open letter to pop music fans

articles.text: Aurora Theatre Company in Berkeley has launched a series of weekly live broadcasts, “Aurora Connects”, online. A broadcast will go live every Friday at 4 p.m. on the theatre company’s YouTube channel. An upcoming episode featuring Maggie Whitaker and Cliff Carruthers will premiere this Friday, July 24. Whitaker is a costume designer with numerous Broadway, film, television, and international credits. Carruthers is a sound designer with a particular talent for working on plays and creating complex sound worlds for complicated texts. He is currently a lecturer at San Francisco State University, and previously lectured at Stanford University. Each episode is hosted by Aurora’s Artistic Director Josh Costello and Associate Artistic Director Dawn Monique Williams. Costello was appointed artistic director in 2019 following a national search. articles.text: Maestro Michael Morgan in rehearsals with Oakland Symphony musicians for Louise Farrenc’s Symphony No. 3. Oakland Symphony is offering a weekly, archival concert series featuring past performances, to debut every Friday at 6 p.m. This week’s episode is Louise Farrenc’s Symphony No.3 in G minor, Op. 36, originally premiered on March 22, 2019 at the Paramount Theatre. The selected music is from the Romantic Period – in the case of Farrenc, the early Romantic Period. “Over the years, we’ve played a series of pieces we’ve called lost romantics,” explained the symphony’s artistic director Michael Morgan. “I’ve heard Louise Farrenc described as ‘criminally underplayed’ and I agree. A revered teacher and performer at the Paris Conservatory, it is said that on the success of this symphony, she demanded and finally got pay that was equal to her male colleagues.” The symphony was originally written by Farrenc in 1847. You can listen to this week’s archival concert at https://www.oaklandsymphony.org/repast/.
articles.title: Oakland Symphony opens archives with “rePAST” concert series

articles.text: Opera San Jose is presenting Schumann’s Dichterliebe with baritone Eugene Brancoveanu Opera San Jose is currently presenting a recital of Robert Schumann’s Dichterliebe (“A Poet’s Love”) for virtual streaming through August 15. The opera will feature resident artist, baritone Eugene Brancoveanu, and resident conductor Christopher James Ray. “The timeless beauty of the music speaks for itself,” Brancoveanu said. “It is at one turn minimalist before raging into a full orchestral sounding polyphony of boisterous emotions and eruptions.” Tickets are “pay what you choose,” with a recommended $15 - $50 per household. Viewing instructions will be accessible after an order confirmation. The run time is approximately 30 minutes, followed by a 15-minute interview with the artists. Opera San Jose is utilizing its Fred Heiman Digital Media Studio, which can serve as both a rehearsal and chamber performance space and be streamed to remote audiences. Dichterliebe is the first concert to be streamed in this way. “With this new space we will be able to safely perform smaller scale operas with theatrical lighting, sets, and appropriate musical accompaniment, utilizing stateof-the-art cameras and audio equipment to create works that can be enjoyed by at-home audiences. This thrilling new venture will enable us to continue our work as an incubator for emerging artists and producer of accessible, world-class operatic performances, while maintaining mitigation efforts to avoid the spread of COVID-19,” said General Director Khori Dastoor. To view the opera, visit https:// www.operasj.org/dichterliebe/.
articles.title: Opera San Jose streams Schumann’s Dichterliebe

articles.text: Brock the parrot sings the blues with San Francisco-based trio Dirty Cello. The Oakland Zoo, after an unprecedented 121-day closure, will reopen to the general public on July 29. Receiving a variance from Alameda County and the State of California to classify the zoo as an outdoor museum was the biggest hurdle to re-opening the zoo, confirmed Neeta Balram, Public Information Manager with the Alameda County Public Health Department. “The Healthcare Services Agency [in Alameda], on the direction of County Board of Supervisors, submitted a letter to the state to consider the zoo an outdoor museum rather than a zoo,” she said. At the time, the Oakland Zoo was the only zoo in the state that could not re-open. The county needed approval from the state after it appeared on the state’s COVID-19 monitoring list, signifying a spike in cases. When East Bay residents learned of this hurdle, they jumped at the chance to support the zoo’s reclassification as an outdoor museum. Caephren McKenna, a firstgrade teacher at Frank Otis Elementary School in Alameda, created a petition on change.org urging Gov. Gavin Newsom to allow Oakland Zoo to reopen as an outdoor museum. The petition quickly collected 2,480 signatures. “Our entire class, 100 students, goes to the zoo every year. It’s definitely a highlight for the kids. It’s a great resource and educational place for the public,” McKenna said. Back Yard Miracle – the ups and downs of hillside retaining walls By Jim Gardner When building outdoor landscaping projects in hillside settings, there are a number of challenges – along with amazing possibilities – that one should consider. This detailed example of a recent extensive retaining wall and patio project should show how these issues came to light and how they were dealt with over the course of a yearlong project. The initial scope of work was to replace a 9-foot tall block retaining wall and patio that was beginning to fail. This impressive home in the Oakland hills was rebuilt after the fire, but as is typical, things like drainage work and retaining walls in the yard were a lower priority compared to the main house. Poor detailing and inexpensive construction were not holding up to the test of time. Without any reinforcement or real footings, this large block wall was starting to shift downhill and the patio had sunk, exaggerated by a lack of appropriate drainage. During the design phase the owner decided to create a lower patio as well. This required another 9-foot wall, but the planning and zoning department would only allow a 6-foot height for any new walls. We decided to create a shorter 3-foot wall at the front for a planting area, with a 6-foot wall at the bottom of the lower patio. The plan was to build a set of new reinforced curved concrete walls and stairs that were faced with stone. This required a fair amount of engineering to start. The new walls required reinStonework was installed. Photos by Jim Gardner Construction The plan was to build new reinforced concrete walls and stairs that were faced with stone. Installation of a membrane, piping and gravel for drainage. READ IT IN THE POST Custom railings were added. forced concrete piers averaging a depth of 13 feet. Unfortunately, the drilling was time consuming, ironically because the soil was good and hard, with the drilling slowing substantially below the 9’ mark. Since drillers are paid by the hour, this added to the cost as the last 4-feet or so and took about twice as long to drill as the first 9 feet. Because of the steep rear yard and limited access via stairs from the front, the holes had to be drilled with a portable rig, which was slow and time consuming to move around. The drilling alone took around 2 months to complete. Once the piers were reinforced and concrete was poured, we began the process of installing the rebar and forms for the footings to the concrete walls connecting between the piers. As you can in the photos, the amount of steel was extensive. All of the materials had to be brought to the site down a long stairway on one side of the house. To facilitate that process, we installed a series of large plastic tubes to bring material down to the job (primarily gravel) and larger 24” diameter tubes at the bottom of the site to carry dirt down to the street below and into a large dump trailer. At the bottom of the site the yard dropped off at an extreme slope. After excavating for the lower 6-foot wall we realized that we were too close to the edge of the drop-off on one side, so we had to add a fourth wall, 6-feet tall on one end, that was tied into our original lower wall to help stabilize it. By the end of the job, we ended up drilling over 50 piers in total. Once the new walls were poured, we installed a membrane, piping and gravel for drainage. Conduits were installed for lighting and irrigation. The spaces behind the walls were backfilled, and reinforced concrete was poured for the patio and stairs. Stonework was installed to face the upper 2 walls, along with slate for the patio. Stone caps were fabricated on-site for the walls. Custom railings were fabricated and installed for the taller walls and stairs. Landscaping, lighting and irrigation were put in as the final touches. Thoughts upon completion There are several takeaways from this work that are important to consider for hillside structural and landscaping projects. The requirements to design and create a properly engineered job that will stand the test of time can be significant. Pier drilling may be slow, especially with portable equipment. Excavation can affect the area adjacent to the site if the space is limited and the grade is steep (it required us to build an additional wall). Access to the site can be a major factor in how long the project lasts. Carting tons of materials back and forth via a long set of stairs added substantial time to the job. Custom curved walls, footings and railings are slow and expensive to produce in comparison to rectangular structures. The bottom line is that you have to consider the site conditions carefully when planning a large project such as this. Given the serious slopes and tall walls, this approach was necessary here. For projects with less severe conditions and options for doing shorter (non-structural) tiered walls, there may be block or rock wall options. For non-engineered walls (typically shorter than 4 feet), that would dramatically simplify the job, particularly when the walls are not close to the house and are more landscaping in nature. This article was written by Jim Gardner of Jim Gardner Construction Inc. Jim is a long-time Piedmont resident and has been doing structural repair in your neighborhood since 1983. articles.text: Armed purse snatcher on Arbor On Friday, July 10, a man armed with a firearm wearing a gray hoodie and a dark colored Covid- 19 mask robbed a woman of her purse in front of her home on Arbor Drive at 7:07 p.m. Items stolen included a credit card, driver’s license, and two iPhone 8s, with a total value of approximately $900. The suspect was seen running down Arbor Drive, jumping in the passenger side of a white vehicle, and escaping. The suspect’s license number was captured on the City’s plate reading cameras and a follow-up by detectives is in progress. Man caught with 2 stolen cars Shortly after 12 noon on Saturday, July 11 the license plate reader at Grand Ave. was triggered by a stolen 1994 Acura Integra. Officers found the car on Cambridge Way with a man standing next to it. Parked behind the vehicle was a Honda Prelude with a female in it. Both vehicles were confirmed as having been stolen. The man and the woman were identified and cited for two counts auto theft, possession of burglary tools, mail theft, possession of stolen property and misappropriation of property. Mail addressed to another person was found in the car. Sergio Flores, 33, of Hayward, was cited and released due to COVID-19 jail capacity concerns. The woman was also cited and released. Thief caught with stolen car, catalytic converters On Monday morning July 13, at 6:53 a.m., a 2004 Chevy Monte Carlo set off the automatic license plate reader eastbound on Wildwood. The car was listed as stolen, and an officer conducted a high-risk traffic stop. Officers detained and handcuffed the female in the passenger seat, but the driver ran away. Five minutes later the suspect was found hiding in a resident’s vehicle. A search of the stolen Monte Carlo revealed a portable Milwaukee Sawzall and four catalytic converters. William Casados, 36, from Hayward, admitted to driving the car and claimed he stole the converters from a junkyard in Hayward. Casados was arrested for possession of a stolen vehicle and stolen property and was sent to Santa Rita jail. The female passenger was released. She was arrested for burglary and conspiracy, sent to Santa Rita jail. The victim suffered a loss of $220 in jewelry lost and $800 in damages to a sliding glass door.

articles.text: California now poised to have more cases than any other state as COVID-19 continues its spread Three more cases of COVID- 19 were added to the count amongst Piedmont residents within the past week, raising the total for Piedmont to 20 as of July 21. This is in addition to four cases reported earlier in July. Three were reported in May and 10 were reported prior to April 13, when the county began delineating cases by cities. The caseload for Alameda County is now 9,383, the highest in the greater Bay Area. More than 1,000 new cases have been added in one week, according to the Alameda County Public Health Department. A total of 167 people have died in the county due to COVID-19, the respiratory disease caused by the novel coronavirus, this year in the county. Oakland now has 3,687 cases, Hayward has 1,379. Fremont has reported 483 cases, San Leandro has reported 474 cases and Berkeley, which has its own Health Department, has a total of 332 cases. Alameda County, the hardest hit in the Bay Area, was placed on the State’s COVID-19 “watchlist” on Sunday, July 12. Counties on the watchlist cannot allow indoor activities like dining and museums. Alameda County had abruptly shut down outdoor dining on Saturday, July 11, but issued a notice on Wednesday, July 15, that allowed outdoor restaurant dining to resume. Of particular note, County officials notified Oakland Zoo on July 15 that it had been approved as an outdoor museum and that it could reopen for outdoor activities. Efforts to reopen more sectors of the economy in Alameda County were halted by officials at the end of June. California has seen a surge of cases in recent weeks and on Monday, July 13, the state ordered the closure of many indoor businesses, from restaurants to movie theaters. After California appeared to slow down the rate of COVID-19 spreading for weeks, cases surged upward in June and July. Now the state is poised to soon have more cases than any other state in the U.S., including New York, the leader for several months. As of yesterday, there have been at least 401,000 cases in California according to a New York Times database, and 7,776 people have died. On Thursday, July 16, the Piedmont Board of Education announced the upcoming school year would have 100 percent remote learning. A day later, Gov. Gavin Newsom ordered that all public and private schools on the state watchlist must continue remote learning until their respective county has been off the watchlist for 14 days. This guidance was echoed by Alameda County officials. The City of Piedmont keeps all of its pandemic-related information available on a webpage at www.piedmont.ca.gov/ government/covid-19.
